decks.title: Reflection — Part 1: Images in the axes, the origin and lines parallel to the axes
goals: Describe a reflection: the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of a point and its image
Write the image of a point reflected in the x-axis, the y-axis or the origin
Write the image of a point reflected in a line x = a or y = b
Work backwards to find a point, a mirror line or unknown coordinates

slides.heading: Reflection, Part 1
slides.body_md: A **reflection** makes a mirror image: every point moves to the other side of a **mirror line**, the same distance away. On a graph the coordinates of the image follow simple rules.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with vertices at (1, 2), (4, 1) and (3, 5) to the right of the y-axis, and its mirror image A′B′C′ at (−1, 2), (−4, 1) and (−3, 5) to the left of the y-axis.
visual.caption: Each vertex of the image is as far behind the mirror as the vertex is in front of it.

slides.narration: Welcome to reflection. When you stand in front of a mirror, your image appears just as far behind it. On a graph we can do the same with points. Here a triangle on the right of the y axis has a mirror image on the left. In this part you will learn the rules that give the coordinates of any image.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Explain what a **reflection** does to a point
Reflect a point in the **$x$-axis**, the **$y$-axis** and the **origin**
Reflect a point in a line **$x = a$** or **$y = b$**
Find a point, a **mirror line** or **unknown coordinates** from given images
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we see exactly what a reflection does. Then we learn the rules for the two axes and for the origin. Next come mirror lines parallel to the axes. Finally we work backwards, finding a point, a mirror line or unknown coordinates from an image.

slides.heading: What a reflection does
slides.body_md: The image $P'$ of a point $P$ in a mirror line lies on the other side of the line, so that the mirror is the **perpendicular bisector** of $PP'$.
bullets: $PP'$ crosses the mirror **at right angles**
the mirror cuts $PP'$ **in half**: $P$ and $P'$ are the same distance from it
a point **on** the mirror is its own image: it is **invariant**

visual.alt: A point P at (4, 3) above a dashed mirror line y = 1, and its image P′ at (4, −1) below it. The segment PP′ is vertical, crosses the mirror at right angles at M (4, 1), and M is 2 units from each end.
visual.caption: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$: $PM = MP' = 2$.

slides.narration: Here the mirror is the line y equals one. The point P is two units above it, so its image P prime is two units below it. The segment joining them crosses the mirror at right angles and is cut exactly in half. A point lying on the mirror itself does not move at all. We call it invariant.

slides.heading: Reflection in the x-axis
slides.body_md: The $x$-axis is the line $y = 0$. Reflecting in it keeps the $x$-coordinate and **changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate**. This reflection is often written $M_x$.

visual.alt: Three points A (2, 3), B (−4, 1) and C (5, −2) joined by vertical segments to their images in the x-axis: A′ (2, −3), B′ (−4, −1) and C′ (5, 2). Each segment is cut in half by the x-axis.
visual.caption: In the $x$-axis: same $x$-coordinate, opposite $y$-coordinate.

slides.narration: Reflect in the x axis and a point above the axis goes the same distance below it, and the other way round. Its x coordinate does not change, but its y coordinate changes sign. So A at two, three goes to two, minus three, and C at five, minus two goes to five, two.

slides.heading: Reflection in the y-axis
slides.body_md: The $y$-axis is the line $x = 0$. Reflecting in it **changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate** and keeps the $y$-coordinate. This reflection is often written $M_y$.

visual.alt: The same three points A (2, 3), B (−4, 1) and C (5, −2) joined by horizontal segments to their images in the y-axis: A′ (−2, 3), B′ (4, 1) and C′ (−5, −2). Each segment is cut in half by the y-axis.
visual.caption: In the $y$-axis: opposite $x$-coordinate, same $y$-coordinate.

slides.narration: Now the mirror is the y axis. A point to the right goes the same distance to the left. This time the y coordinate stays the same and the x coordinate changes sign. So A at two, three goes to minus two, three, and B at minus four, one goes to four, one.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: images in the axes
slides.body_md: Write the images of $A(-5, 2)$ and $B(0, -3)$ under reflection in (i) the $x$-axis, (ii) the $y$-axis.
bullets: **Step 1 —** in the $x$-axis change the sign of $y$: $A$ goes to $(-5, -2)$ and $B$ to $(0, 3)$.
**Step 2 —** in the $y$-axis change the sign of $x$: $A$ goes to $(5, 2)$; $B$ goes to $(0, -3)$, itself.
**Note —** $B$ lies on the $y$-axis, so it is **invariant** under reflection in the $y$-axis.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: A (−5, 2) has image (−5, −2) in the x-axis and (5, 2) in the y-axis; B (0, −3) has image (0, 3) in the x-axis and stays at (0, −3) in the y-axis, because it lies on the y-axis.
visual.caption: A point on the mirror does not move.

slides.narration: For the x axis, change the sign of the y coordinate: A goes to minus five, minus two and B goes to zero, three. For the y axis, change the sign of the x coordinate: A goes to five, two. But B has x coordinate zero, so changing its sign changes nothing. B lies on the mirror and stays where it is.

slides.heading: Quick check: the y-axis
slides.body_md: Which coordinate changes sign?
slides.narration: The mirror is the y axis. Which coordinate changes sign, and which stays the same?

slides.heading: Reflection in the origin
slides.body_md: Reflection in the origin **changes the signs of both coordinates**. The origin is the midpoint of $PP'$. It has the same effect as reflecting in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis. It is often written $M_O$.

visual.alt: A point P at (3, 2) and its image P′ at (−3, −2) under reflection in the origin. The segment PP′ passes through the origin O, which is its midpoint.
visual.caption: The origin is the midpoint of $PP'$.

slides.narration: We can also reflect in a point, the origin. The image is as far beyond the origin as the point is in front of it, on the same straight line. Both coordinates change sign, so three, two goes to minus three, minus two. This is the same as reflecting in the x axis and then in the y axis.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: working back
slides.body_md: The image of a point $P$ in the $y$-axis is $(-6, -1)$. Find $P$, and the image of $P$ in the origin.
bullets: **Step 1 —** a reflection undoes itself: reflect $(-6, -1)$ in the $y$-axis again to get $P(6, -1)$.
**Step 2 —** in the origin both signs change: the image of $P$ is $(-6, 1)$.
**Check —** $(6, -1)$ in the $y$-axis gives $(-6, -1)$, the given image.

visual.alt: Worked example 2: the given image P′ (−6, −1), the point P (6, −1) found by reflecting it back in the y-axis, and Q (−6, 1), the image of P in the origin; the segment PQ passes through the origin.
visual.caption: Reflect the image back to find the point; then change both signs.

slides.narration: If we know an image, reflecting it in the same mirror takes us back to the point. So P is six, minus one. Its image in the origin changes both signs, giving minus six, one. Always check by reflecting your answer forwards again.

slides.heading: Quick check: working backwards
slides.body_md: Reflect the image in the same mirror.
slides.narration: To find the point, reflect the given image in the same mirror line.

slides.heading: Reflection in the line x = a
slides.body_md: A **vertical** mirror $x = a$ keeps the $y$-coordinate. A point $x - a$ to the right of the mirror goes the same distance to its left, so its new $x$-coordinate is

visual.alt: A dashed vertical mirror x = 2. P (5, 3) is 3 units to its right and its image P′ (−1, 3) is 3 units to its left; Q (0, −2) is 2 units to its left and its image Q′ (4, −2) is 2 units to its right.
visual.caption: Same distance on each side of $x = 2$; the $y$-coordinate is kept.

slides.narration: Now the mirror is a vertical line, x equals a. The y coordinate stays the same. A point three units to the right of the mirror ends up three units to the left of it. In symbols the new x coordinate is two a minus x. For the mirror x equals two, the point five, three goes to minus one, three.

slides.heading: Reflection in the line y = b
slides.body_md: A **horizontal** mirror $y = b$ keeps the $x$-coordinate, and the new $y$-coordinate is $2b - y$.

visual.alt: A dashed horizontal mirror y = −1. P (2, 3) is 4 units above it and its image P′ (2, −5) is 4 units below; Q (−3, −2) is 1 unit below it and its image Q′ (−3, 0) is 1 unit above.
visual.caption: Same distance above and below $y = -1$; the $x$-coordinate is kept.

slides.narration: A horizontal mirror, y equals b, works the same way with the roles swapped. The x coordinate stays the same, and the new y coordinate is two b minus y. With the mirror y equals minus one, the point two, three, which is four units above, goes to two, minus five, four units below.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: lines parallel to the axes
slides.body_md: Find the images of $R(7, -2)$ in (i) the line $x = 3$, (ii) the line $y = 1$.
bullets: **(i) —** $y$ stays $-2$; new $x$-coordinate $2 \times 3 - 7 = -1$: the image is $(-1, -2)$.
**(ii) —** $x$ stays $7$; new $y$-coordinate $2 \times 1 - (-2) = 4$: the image is $(7, 4)$.
**Check —** in each case the mirror is halfway between the point and its image.

visual.alt: Worked example 3: R (7, −2) with its image R′ (−1, −2) in the dashed vertical mirror x = 3, joined by a horizontal segment, and its image R″ (7, 4) in the dashed horizontal mirror y = 1, joined by a vertical segment.
visual.caption: A vertical mirror moves the point sideways; a horizontal mirror moves it up or down.

slides.narration: For the vertical mirror x equals three, keep the y coordinate and work out two times three minus seven, which is minus one. For the horizontal mirror y equals one, keep the x coordinate and work out two times one minus minus two, which is four. Check that each mirror lies halfway between the point and its image.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: finding the mirror
slides.body_md: Find the mirror line in each case: (i) $P(-1, 6)$ and its image $P'(-1, -2)$; (ii) $Q(5, 4)$ and its image $Q'(-3, 4)$.
bullets: **(i) —** same $x$-coordinate, so the mirror is horizontal, halfway between: $y = \dfrac{6 + (-2)}{2} = 2$.
**(ii) —** same $y$-coordinate, so the mirror is vertical, halfway between: $x = \dfrac{5 + (-3)}{2} = 1$.
**Answer —** the mirrors are $y = 2$ and $x = 1$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4: the vertical segment from P (−1, 6) to P′ (−1, −2) is bisected by the dashed horizontal mirror y = 2, and the horizontal segment from Q (5, 4) to Q′ (−3, 4) is bisected by the dashed vertical mirror x = 1.
visual.caption: The mirror passes through the midpoint of the segment, at right angles to it.

slides.narration: The mirror passes through the midpoint of a point and its image, at right angles to the segment joining them. In the first pair the x coordinates are equal, so the mirror is horizontal, at the average height, two. In the second pair the y coordinates are equal, so the mirror is vertical, at x equals one.

slides.heading: Quick check: the mirror line
slides.body_md: Take the average of the coordinates that change.
slides.narration: The two points share their x coordinate. The mirror is halfway between their y coordinates.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: unknown coordinates
slides.body_md: The image of $(2a - 3, 5)$ in the $y$-axis is $(-7, b + 2)$. Find $a$ and $b$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** by the rule, the image is $(3 - 2a, 5)$.
**Step 2 —** compare $x$-coordinates: $3 - 2a = -7 \Rightarrow 2a = 10 \Rightarrow a = 5$.
**Step 3 —** compare $y$-coordinates: $b + 2 = 5 \Rightarrow b = 3$.
**Check —** the point is $(7, 5)$, whose image in the $y$-axis is $(-7, 5)$.

nodes.label: Write the image by the rule
Equate the $x$-coordinates
Equate the $y$-coordinates
Substitute back to check

visual.alt: Flow chart for unknown coordinates: write the image of the given point using the reflection rule, set its x-coordinate equal to the given x-coordinate, set its y-coordinate equal to the given y-coordinate, then substitute the values back to check.
visual.caption: Two equal points have equal $x$-coordinates and equal $y$-coordinates.

slides.narration: First write the image using the rule: the x coordinate changes sign, so it becomes three minus two a, and the y coordinate stays five. Two points are equal only when both coordinates match. So three minus two a equals minus seven, giving a equals five, and b plus two equals five, giving b equals three.

slides.heading: All the rules together
slides.body_md: Learn the five rules and which points each one leaves fixed:

visual.alt: Table of the five reflections with the image of the point (4, −3): in the x-axis (4, 3); in the y-axis (−4, −3); in the origin (−4, 3); in the line x = 1, (−2, −3); in the line y = 2, (4, 7). The x-axis, the y-axis and the lines keep every point on them fixed; the origin keeps only itself fixed.
visual.caption: Five rules, one example point.

slides.narration: Here are all five rules in one table, with the image of the point four, minus three under each. A line mirror leaves every point on it fixed. Reflection in the origin leaves only the origin fixed. Learn the table, and you can answer most reflection questions in one line.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: How far is the point from the mirror?
slides.narration: Find how far the point is from the mirror, then go the same distance beyond it.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$
$x$-axis: $(x, -y)$; $y$-axis: $(-x, y)$; origin: $(-x, -y)$
Line $x = a$: $(2a - x, y)$; line $y = b$: $(x, 2b - y)$
Reflect an image again to get the point back
Mirror from a point and its image: halfway between them

visual.alt: The point P (3, 2) with its images in the x-axis (3, −2), the origin (−3, −2) and the y-axis (−3, 2); the four points are the corners of a rectangle centred on the origin.
visual.caption: One point, three images: the corners of a rectangle.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of a point and its image. In the x axis the y coordinate changes sign; in the y axis the x coordinate does; in the origin both do. For lines parallel to the axes use two a minus x or two b minus y. And to work backwards, reflect again.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Image of a point (1 mark each):** correct coordinates, written as a pair
**Mirror line (1–2 marks):** horizontal or vertical stated, then the equation
**Unknown coordinates (2–3 marks):** image by the rule 1 + each equation solved 1
**Mistake:** changing the wrong coordinate (the $x$-axis changes $y$)
**Mistake:** using $a - x$ instead of $2a - x$ for the line $x = a$
**Mistake:** writing a mirror line such as $y = 3$ as $x = 3$
slides.narration: In the exam, write each image as a coordinate pair. For a mirror line, say first whether it is horizontal or vertical, then give its equation. A very common slip is to change the wrong coordinate: reflection in the x axis changes the y coordinate. And for the line x equals a, the new x coordinate is two a minus x.

decks.title: Reflection — Part 2: Invariant points, combined reflections and figures
goals: Identify the invariant points of a reflection
Combine two reflections and find a single equivalent reflection
Reflect a figure and plot it with its image on graph paper
Name the figure formed and find its area or perimeter

slides.heading: Reflection, Part 2
slides.body_md: Reflect a whole figure and it keeps its size and shape but **faces the other way**. Points and their images together make new figures to name and measure.

visual.alt: A flag on a pole to the right of the y-axis, with its tip F at (5, 4), and its mirror image to the left with the tip F′ at (−5, 4). The image flag points the other way.
visual.caption: A reflected figure is the same size and shape, but faces the other way.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here a flag on a pole is reflected in the y axis. The image flag is exactly the same size and shape, but it points the other way. In this part we look at points that do not move, at doing two reflections in a row, and at the shapes that points and their images make on graph paper.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **invariant points** of a reflection
Combine **two reflections** into one
Reflect a **figure** and plot it with its image
**Name** the figure formed and find its **area** or **perimeter**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We find which points stay fixed, combine two reflections, reflect whole figures, and then name the shapes formed on graph paper and work out their areas and perimeters.

slides.heading: Invariant points
slides.body_md: A point is **invariant** under a reflection if it is its own image. For a mirror **line**, the invariant points are exactly the points **on the line**. For reflection in the **origin**, only the origin itself is invariant.

visual.alt: A dashed mirror y = −2 with two points U (−3, −2) and V (2, −2) on it, which stay where they are, and a point W (1, 1) above it that moves to W′ (1, −5) below it.
visual.caption: Points on the mirror are invariant; every other point moves.

slides.narration: A point is invariant if its image is the point itself. For a mirror line, that happens exactly when the point lies on the line. Here U and V sit on the mirror y equals minus two, so they stay put, while W moves to the other side. For reflection in the origin, only the origin is invariant.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which points stay fixed?
slides.body_md: Which of $A(3, 0)$, $B(0, -2)$, $C(-2, 5)$, $D(-2, -2)$ are invariant under reflection in (i) the $x$-axis, (ii) the $y$-axis, (iii) the line $x = -2$, (iv) the line $y = -2$?
bullets: **Step 1 —** a point is invariant exactly when it lies on the mirror.
**Answers —** (i) $A$; (ii) $B$; (iii) $C$ and $D$; (iv) $B$ and $D$.
**Note —** $D$ is invariant under both $x = -2$ and $y = -2$: it is where the two lines cross.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1 of part 2: under the x-axis only A is invariant; under the y-axis only B; under the line x = −2 the points C and D; under the line y = −2 the points B and D. D is invariant under both lines.
visual.caption: $D(-2, -2)$ lies on both $x = -2$ and $y = -2$.

slides.narration: Check which points lie on each mirror. A has y coordinate zero, so it is on the x axis. B has x coordinate zero, so it is on the y axis. C and D have x coordinate minus two. B and D have y coordinate minus two. D lies on both of the last two lines, at their crossing point.

slides.heading: Quick check: invariant points
slides.body_md: Which point lies on the mirror?
slides.narration: Look for the point that lies on the y axis. What is its x coordinate?

slides.heading: One reflection after another
slides.body_md: Reflecting in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis (in either order) changes both signs, which is **reflection in the origin**. Reflecting **twice in the same line** brings every point back.

series.label: in the x-axis, then in the y-axis

visual.alt: The point P (4, 2) is reflected in the x-axis to P1 (4, −2) and then in the y-axis to P2 (−4, −2). A straight segment from P through the origin also reaches P2, showing that the two reflections together equal reflection in the origin.
visual.caption: Two axis reflections, one after the other, equal one reflection in the origin.

slides.narration: Reflect four, two in the x axis to get four, minus two, then in the y axis to get minus four, minus two. Both signs have changed, exactly as for reflection in the origin. So these two reflections together equal one reflection in the origin. And reflecting twice in the same line just brings a point back.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two mirrors
slides.body_md: $P(3, -5)$ is reflected in the line $y = 1$ to $P_1$, and $P_1$ in the $y$-axis to $P_2$. Find $P_2$. Does the other order give the same point?
bullets: **Step 1 —** new $y$-coordinate $2 \times 1 - (-5) = 7$: $P_1(3, 7)$.
**Step 2 —** in the $y$-axis: $P_2(-3, 7)$.
**Other order —** $y$-axis first gives $(-3, -5)$, then $y = 1$ gives $(-3, 7)$: the same point.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 of part 2: P (3, −5) goes to P1 (3, 7) in the line y = 1 and then to P2 (−3, 7) in the y-axis. Taking the y-axis first sends P to Q (−3, −5), and then the line y = 1 sends Q to the same point P2.
visual.caption: For two perpendicular mirrors the order does not matter.

slides.narration: In the line y equals one, the new y coordinate is two times one minus minus five, which is seven. So P one is three, seven. Then the y axis changes the sign of x: P two is minus three, seven. Doing the y axis first gives minus three, minus five, and then seven again. For perpendicular mirrors, the order does not matter.

slides.heading: Reflecting a figure
slides.body_md: To reflect a figure, reflect **each vertex** and join the images in the same order.
bullets: the image is **congruent** to the figure: same lengths, angles and area
vertices on the mirror are **invariant**
the order of the vertices is **reversed** (clockwise becomes anticlockwise)

visual.alt: Triangle KLM with K (2, 1), L (5, 2) and M (3, 4), and its image K′ (0, 1), L′ (−3, 2), M′ (−1, 4) in the dashed mirror x = 1. The two triangles have the same side lengths but face opposite ways.
visual.caption: Reflect every vertex, then join the images in the same order.

slides.narration: To reflect a whole figure, reflect each of its corners and join them up in the same order. The image has the same side lengths, the same angles and the same area, so it is congruent to the original. But it faces the other way: going round the corners clockwise in one means anticlockwise in the other.

slides.heading: Quick check: two routes
slides.body_md: Follow both routes step by step.
slides.narration: Work out the image both ways, step by step, and compare.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a rectangle from one point
slides.body_md: Plot $A(5, 2)$ and its images $B$ in the $y$-axis, $C$ in the origin and $D$ in the $x$-axis. Name $ABCD$ and find its area and perimeter.
bullets: **Step 2 —** the sides are horizontal and vertical, so every angle is a right angle: $AB = 5 - (-5) = 10$ and $BC = 2 - (-2) = 4$, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle.
**Step 3 —** area $10 \times 4 = 40$ square units; perimeter $2 \times (10 + 4) = 28$ units.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 of part 2: A (5, 2) with B (−5, 2), its image in the y-axis, C (−5, −2), its image in the origin, and D (5, −2), its image in the x-axis. ABCD is a rectangle 10 units wide and 4 units tall.
visual.caption: $ABCD$ is a rectangle: $10 \times 4 = 40$ square units.

slides.narration: The three images are minus five, two; minus five, minus two; and five, minus two. Joining A, B, C and D gives horizontal and vertical sides, so all the angles are right angles. The width is ten and the height is four, so it is a rectangle with area forty square units and perimeter twenty eight units.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an isosceles trapezium
slides.body_md: The segment joining $A(1, 4)$ and $B(3, 1)$ is reflected in the line $x = 5$ to $A'B'$. Name $ABB'A'$ and find its area.
bullets: **Step 1 —** new $x$-coordinates $2 \times 5 - 1 = 9$ and $2 \times 5 - 3 = 7$: $A'(9, 4)$, $B'(7, 1)$.
**Step 2 —** $AA'$ and $BB'$ are horizontal, so parallel; $AB = A'B'$. So $ABB'A'$ is an **isosceles trapezium**.
**Step 3 —** $AA' = 9 - 1 = 8$, $BB' = 7 - 3 = 4$, height $4 - 1 = 3$; area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (8 + 4) \times 3 = 18$ square units.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 of part 2: the segment from A (1, 4) to B (3, 1) and its image from A′ (9, 4) to B′ (7, 1) in the dashed mirror x = 5. Together they form a trapezium with horizontal parallel sides AA′ of length 8 and BB′ of length 4, 3 units apart.
visual.caption: Parallel sides $8$ and $4$, height $3$: area $18$ square units.

slides.narration: Reflect both ends in the line x equals five: A goes to nine, four and B goes to seven, one. The segments A A prime and B B prime are both horizontal, so they are parallel, and the slanting sides are a segment and its image, so they are equal. That makes an isosceles trapezium, with area eighteen square units.

slides.heading: Naming the figure
slides.body_md: On graph paper, horizontal and vertical sides make parallel sides and right angles easy to spot. Then check the side lengths:

nodes.label: Both pairs of opposite sides parallel?
All angles right angles?
Exactly one pair parallel?
All sides equal: square; otherwise rectangle
All sides equal: rhombus; otherwise parallelogram
Trapezium (isosceles if the other two sides are equal)
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides: kite

visual.alt: Flow chart for naming a quadrilateral: if both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, check for right angles, giving a square or rectangle, or else a rhombus or parallelogram, depending on whether all sides are equal; if exactly one pair is parallel it is a trapezium, isosceles if the other two sides are equal; otherwise look for two pairs of equal adjacent sides, which make a kite.
visual.caption: Horizontal and vertical sides on graph paper make parallel sides and right angles easy to see.

slides.narration: To name a four sided figure, first look for parallel sides. Two pairs of parallel sides make a parallelogram, and right angles or equal sides turn it into a rectangle, rhombus or square. Exactly one pair makes a trapezium. With no parallel sides, two pairs of equal neighbouring sides make a kite.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a kite
slides.body_md: Reflect $A(-1, 2)$ in the line $x = 2$ to get $C$. With $B(2, 6)$ and $D(2, -1)$, name $ABCD$ and find its area.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $2 \times 2 - (-1) = 5$: $C(5, 2)$. $B$ and $D$ lie on the mirror, so they are invariant.
**Step 2 —** $AB = CB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ and $AD = CD$, but $AB \ne AD$: $ABCD$ is a **kite**.
**Step 3 —** the diagonals $AC = 5 - (-1) = 6$ and $BD = 6 - (-1) = 7$ are perpendicular: area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 7 = 21$ square units.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 of part 2: A (−1, 2) and its image C (5, 2) in the dashed mirror x = 2, with B (2, 6) and D (2, −1) on the mirror. ABCD is a kite whose diagonal BD lies along the mirror and is perpendicular to the diagonal AC.
visual.caption: Diagonals $AC = 6$ and $BD = 7$ cross at right angles: area $21$ square units.

slides.narration: The image of A in the line x equals two is C at five, two. B and D are on the mirror, so they stay fixed. The mirror swaps A and C, so A B equals C B and A D equals C D: two pairs of equal neighbouring sides, a kite. Its diagonals, six and seven, cross at right angles, so the area is twenty one square units.

slides.heading: Quick check: an area

notes.title: Reflection — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Reflection in a mirror line
sections.body_md:
- A **reflection** in a mirror line $l$ sends each point $P$ to its **image** $P'$ on the other side of $l$, at the same distance from it.
- The mirror line is the **perpendicular bisector** of $PP'$: $PP'$ meets $l$ at right angles, and $l$ passes through the midpoint of $PP'$.
- A point and its image are $2k$ units apart when the point is $k$ units from the mirror.
- A point **on** the mirror is its own image (it is **invariant**).

*Example:* $P(4, 3)$ in the line $y = 1$: $P$ is $2$ units above the mirror, so $P'$ is $(4, -1)$, $2$ units below it.

key_terms.definition_md: The point to which a reflection sends a given point.
The line of reflection; it is the perpendicular bisector of every segment $PP'$.

visual.alt: A point P at (4, 3) above a dashed mirror line y = 1, and its image P′ at (4, −1) below it. The segment PP′ is vertical, crosses the mirror at right angles at M (4, 1), and M is 2 units from each end.
visual.caption: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$: $PM = MP' = 2$.

visuals.alt: A triangle ABC with vertices at (1, 2), (4, 1) and (3, 5) to the right of the y-axis, and its mirror image A′B′C′ at (−1, 2), (−4, 1) and (−3, 5) to the left of the y-axis.
visuals.caption: Each vertex of the image is as far behind the mirror as the vertex is in front of it.

sections.heading: 2. Reflection in the axes
sections.body_md:
- **In the $x$-axis** ($y = 0$, written $M_x$): keep $x$, change the sign of $y$.
- **In the $y$-axis** ($x = 0$, written $M_y$): change the sign of $x$, keep $y$.

$$M_x : (x, y) \to (x, -y) \qquad M_y : (x, y) \to (-x, y)$$

*Example:* $A(-5, 2)$ goes to $(-5, -2)$ in the $x$-axis and to $(5, 2)$ in the $y$-axis; $B(0, -3)$ lies on the $y$-axis, so it is invariant under $M_y$.

visual.alt: Three points A (2, 3), B (−4, 1) and C (5, −2) joined by vertical segments to their images in the x-axis: A′ (2, −3), B′ (−4, −1) and C′ (5, 2). Each segment is cut in half by the x-axis.
visual.caption: In the $x$-axis: same $x$-coordinate, opposite $y$-coordinate.

visuals.alt: The same three points A (2, 3), B (−4, 1) and C (5, −2) joined by horizontal segments to their images in the y-axis: A′ (−2, 3), B′ (4, 1) and C′ (−5, −2). Each segment is cut in half by the y-axis.
visuals.caption: In the $y$-axis: opposite $x$-coordinate, same $y$-coordinate.

visuals.alt: Table for worked example 1: A (−5, 2) has image (−5, −2) in the x-axis and (5, 2) in the y-axis; B (0, −3) has image (0, 3) in the x-axis and stays at (0, −3) in the y-axis, because it lies on the y-axis.
visuals.caption: A point on the mirror does not move.

sections.heading: 3. Reflection in the origin
sections.body_md:
- **In the origin** (written $M_O$): change the signs of **both** coordinates. The origin is the midpoint of $PP'$, and $P$, $O$, $P'$ lie on one straight line.

$$M_O : (x, y) \to (-x, -y)$$

- Reflection in the $x$-axis followed by reflection in the $y$-axis (in either order) has the same effect as $M_O$.
- Only the origin is invariant under $M_O$.

*Example:* the image of $(3, 2)$ in the origin is $(-3, -2)$; and if the image of $P$ in the $y$-axis is $(-6, -1)$, then $P$ is $(6, -1)$ and its image in the origin is $(-6, 1)$.

visual.alt: A point P at (3, 2) and its image P′ at (−3, −2) under reflection in the origin. The segment PP′ passes through the origin O, which is its midpoint.
visual.caption: The origin is the midpoint of $PP'$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2: the given image P′ (−6, −1), the point P (6, −1) found by reflecting it back in the y-axis, and Q (−6, 1), the image of P in the origin; the segment PQ passes through the origin.
visuals.caption: Reflect the image back to find the point; then change both signs.

sections.heading: 4. Reflection in the lines x = a and y = b
sections.body_md:
- **In $x = a$** (a vertical mirror): keep $y$; a point $x - a$ to the right goes $x - a$ to the left, so the new $x$-coordinate is $a - (x - a) = 2a - x$.
- **In $y = b$** (a horizontal mirror): keep $x$; the new $y$-coordinate is $2b - y$.

$$(x, y) \to (2a - x, y) \qquad (x, y) \to (x, 2b - y)$$

- With $a = 0$ or $b = 0$ these become the rules for the axes.

*Example:* $R(7, -2)$ goes to $(2 \times 3 - 7, -2) = (-1, -2)$ in $x = 3$ and to $(7, 4)$ in $y = 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: $x = a$ is vertical (parallel to the $y$-axis); $y = b$ is horizontal (parallel to the $x$-axis).

visual.alt: A dashed vertical mirror x = 2. P (5, 3) is 3 units to its right and its image P′ (−1, 3) is 3 units to its left; Q (0, −2) is 2 units to its left and its image Q′ (4, −2) is 2 units to its right.
visual.caption: Same distance on each side of $x = 2$; the $y$-coordinate is kept.

visuals.alt: A dashed horizontal mirror y = −1. P (2, 3) is 4 units above it and its image P′ (2, −5) is 4 units below; Q (−3, −2) is 1 unit below it and its image Q′ (−3, 0) is 1 unit above.
visuals.caption: Same distance above and below $y = -1$; the $x$-coordinate is kept.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3: R (7, −2) with its image R′ (−1, −2) in the dashed vertical mirror x = 3, joined by a horizontal segment, and its image R″ (7, 4) in the dashed horizontal mirror y = 1, joined by a vertical segment.
visuals.caption: A vertical mirror moves the point sideways; a horizontal mirror moves it up or down.

sections.heading: 5. Working backwards
sections.body_md:
- **The point from its image:** a reflection undoes itself, so reflect the image in the same mirror.
- **The mirror from a point and its image:** if the $x$-coordinates are equal, the mirror is horizontal, $y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$; if the $y$-coordinates are equal, it is vertical, $x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$; if both coordinates change sign, it is the origin.
- **Unknown coordinates:** write the image by the rule, then equate $x$-coordinates and $y$-coordinates separately.

*Example:* the image of $(2a - 3, 5)$ in the $y$-axis is $(-7, b + 2)$: $3 - 2a = -7$, so $a = 5$; $b + 2 = 5$, so $b = 3$.

key_terms.definition_md: Reflecting twice in the same mirror gives back the original point.

visual.alt: Worked example 4: the vertical segment from P (−1, 6) to P′ (−1, −2) is bisected by the dashed horizontal mirror y = 2, and the horizontal segment from Q (5, 4) to Q′ (−3, 4) is bisected by the dashed vertical mirror x = 1.
visual.caption: The mirror passes through the midpoint of the segment, at right angles to it.

nodes.label: Write the image by the rule
Equate the $x$-coordinates

Substitute back to check

visuals.alt: Flow chart for unknown coordinates: write the image of the given point using the reflection rule, set its x-coordinate equal to the given x-coordinate, set its y-coordinate equal to the given y-coordinate, then substitute the values back to check.
visuals.caption: Two equal points have equal $x$-coordinates and equal $y$-coordinates.

sections.heading: 6. Invariant points
sections.body_md:
- A point is **invariant** under a reflection if its image is the point itself.
- For a mirror **line**, the invariant points are exactly the points **on** that line: $(x, 0)$ for the $x$-axis, $(0, y)$ for the $y$-axis, $(a, y)$ for $x = a$, $(x, b)$ for $y = b$.
- For the **origin**, only $O(0, 0)$ is invariant.
- A point invariant under two reflections in perpendicular lines is their point of intersection.

*Example:* $D(-2, -2)$ is invariant under reflection in both $x = -2$ and $y = -2$.

key_terms.definition_md: A point that is its own image under a transformation.

visual.alt: A dashed mirror y = −2 with two points U (−3, −2) and V (2, −2) on it, which stay where they are, and a point W (1, 1) above it that moves to W′ (1, −5) below it.
visual.caption: Points on the mirror are invariant; every other point moves.

visuals.alt: Table of the five reflections with the image of the point (4, −3): in the x-axis (4, 3); in the y-axis (−4, −3); in the origin (−4, 3); in the line x = 1, (−2, −3); in the line y = 2, (4, 7). The x-axis, the y-axis and the lines keep every point on them fixed; the origin keeps only itself fixed.
visuals.caption: Five rules, one example point.

visuals.alt: Table for worked example 1 of part 2: under the x-axis only A is invariant; under the y-axis only B; under the line x = −2 the points C and D; under the line y = −2 the points B and D. D is invariant under both lines.
visuals.caption: $D(-2, -2)$ lies on both $x = -2$ and $y = -2$.

sections.heading: 7. Combined reflections and figures on graph paper
sections.body_md:
- **Two reflections:** $x$-axis then $y$-axis (either order) $=$ reflection in the origin; the same mirror twice $=$ no change.
- **A figure:** reflect each vertex and join the images in the same order. The image is **congruent** (same lengths, angles, area) but the order of the vertices is reversed.
- **Naming the figure:** horizontal and vertical sides give parallel sides and right angles at a glance; then compare side lengths (rectangle, square, isosceles trapezium, kite, right-angled or isosceles triangle).
- **Area:** use horizontal or vertical sides as bases and heights; trapezium $\dfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h$; kite $\dfrac{1}{2} d_1 d_2$.

*Example:* $A(5, 2)$ with its images in the $y$-axis, the origin and the $x$-axis makes a rectangle $10$ by $4$: area $40$ square units, perimeter $28$ units.

key_terms.definition_md: Same size and shape; a reflected figure is congruent to the original.
A trapezium whose non-parallel sides are equal; a segment and its image often make one.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 of part 2: A (5, 2) with B (−5, 2), its image in the y-axis, C (−5, −2), its image in the origin, and D (5, −2), its image in the x-axis. ABCD is a rectangle 10 units wide and 4 units tall.
visual.caption: $ABCD$ is a rectangle: $10 \times 4 = 40$ square units.

visuals.alt: The point P (4, 2) is reflected in the x-axis to P1 (4, −2) and then in the y-axis to P2 (−4, −2). A straight segment from P through the origin also reaches P2, showing that the two reflections together equal reflection in the origin.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Image of a point (1 mark):* correct coordinate pair.
- *Mirror line from a point and its image (1–2 marks):* horizontal or vertical stated 1; equation 1.
- *Unknown coordinates (2–3 marks):* image by the rule 1; each unknown 1.
- *Invariant points (1–2 marks):* the points on the mirror, with a reason.
- *10-mark graph question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually 3 + 3 + 4: plotting and labelling, images, naming the figure with a reason, area or perimeter; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Changing the wrong coordinate: reflection in the $x$-axis changes the $y$-coordinate.
2. Using $a - x$ or $x - 2a$ instead of $2a - x$ for the line $x = a$.
3. Confusing the line $x = 3$ (vertical) with the line $y = 3$ (horizontal).
4. Saying a point on the $x$-axis is invariant under reflection in the $y$-axis (only the origin is).
5. Joining the vertices of a figure in the wrong order, or naming it without a reason.
6. Forgetting the half in the area of a triangle, trapezium or kite.

cards.front_md: What is the **image** of a point under a reflection?
cards.back_md: The point on the other side of the mirror line, at the same distance from it, with the mirror as the perpendicular bisector of the joining segment.

cards.front_md: What is an **invariant point**?
cards.back_md: A point that is its own image under the transformation.

cards.front_md: Rule for reflection in the **$x$-axis**?
cards.back_md: $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$: keep $x$, change the sign of $y$.

cards.front_md: Rule for reflection in the **$y$-axis**?
cards.back_md: $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$: change the sign of $x$, keep $y$.

cards.front_md: Rule for reflection in the **origin**?
cards.back_md: $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$: change both signs.

questions.stem_md: Under reflection in the $x$-axis, the point $(5, -7)$ is mapped to
questions.solution_md: Reflection in the $x$-axis keeps the $x$-coordinate and changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate: $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$, so $(5, -7)$ goes to $(5, 7)$. Option (b) is the image in the $y$-axis, (c) the image in the origin, and (d) swaps the coordinates.

questions.stem_md: Which point is the mirror image of $Q(-4, 9)$ when the $y$-axis acts as the mirror?
questions.solution_md: Reflection in the $y$-axis changes only the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$, so the image is $(4, 9)$. Option (c) is the image in the $x$-axis and (d) the image in the origin.

questions.stem_md: Reflection in the origin sends $R(6, -2)$ to which point?
questions.solution_md: Reflection in the origin changes the signs of both coordinates: $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$, giving $(-6, 2)$. Option (d) is the image in the $x$-axis and (a) the image in the $y$-axis; (b) swaps the coordinates as well.

questions.stem_md: A vertical mirror stands along the line $x = 4$. Where is the image of $A(7, 3)$?
questions.solution_md: The $y$-coordinate stays $3$, and the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 4 - 7 = 1$: $A$ is $3$ units to the right of the mirror, so its image is $3$ units to the left. Option (c) adds $4$ to $7$, (a) reflects in the line $y = 4$ instead, and (b) uses the $y$-axis as the mirror.

questions.stem_md: What are the coordinates of the image of $B(-2, 5)$ when it is reflected in the horizontal line $y = -1$?
questions.solution_md: The $x$-coordinate stays $-2$, and the new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times (-1) - 5 = -7$: $B$ is $5 - (-1) = 6$ units above the mirror, so the image is $6$ units below it. Option (b) reflects in the $x$-axis, (c) works out $2 \times (-1) + 5$, and (d) reflects in the line $x = -1$.

questions.stem_md: After reflection in the $x$-axis, a point $P$ lands at $P'(-3, -8)$. Where was $P$?
questions.solution_md: Reflecting $P'$ in the $x$-axis again gives back $P$, so $P$ is $(-3, 8)$. Option (c) is the image of $P'$ in the $y$-axis, and (d) its image in the origin.

questions.stem_md: Which of these points does not move (is invariant) when the plane is reflected in the $y$-axis?
questions.solution_md: A point is invariant under reflection in the $y$-axis exactly when it lies on the $y$-axis, that is, when its $x$-coordinate is $0$. Only $(0, -6)$ qualifies; $(-6, 0)$ lies on the $x$-axis and moves to $(6, 0)$.

questions.stem_md: A mirror is placed along the line $y = 3$. Which point coincides with its own image?
questions.solution_md: Only points on the mirror line are their own images. Every point of the line $y = 3$ has $y$-coordinate $3$, so $(-5, 3)$ is invariant. Option (a) has $x$-coordinate $3$, which puts it on the line $x = 3$, not on $y = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A point is reflected in the $x$-axis, and its image is then reflected in the $y$-axis. Which single reflection has the same overall effect?
questions.solution_md: $(x, y) \to (x, -y) \to (-x, -y)$: both signs change, which is exactly reflection in the origin. For example, $(4, 1) \to (4, -1) \to (-4, -1)$.

questions.stem_md: The point $(4, -1)$ is the image of $(4, 7)$ in a mirror line. What is the equation of the mirror line?
questions.solution_md: The $x$-coordinates are equal, so the mirror is horizontal and lies halfway between the two points: $\dfrac{7 + (-1)}{2} = 3$. The mirror is $y = 3$. Option (d) works out $\dfrac{7 + 1}{2} = 4$, ignoring the minus sign, and (a) is the distance $7 - (-1) = 8$ between the points.

questions.stem_md: Reflection in the line $x = -2$ takes a point $M$ to $M'(3, -4)$. What are the coordinates of $M$?
questions.solution_md: Reflecting $M'$ in the same line gives back $M$. The $y$-coordinate stays $-4$, and the $x$-coordinate is $2 \times (-2) - 3 = -7$. Option (d) uses the line $x = 2$, (a) uses the $y$-axis, and (b) reflects in the line $y = -2$.

questions.stem_md: $P(2, -6)$ is reflected in the origin to give $P_1$, and $P_1$ is then reflected in the $x$-axis to give $P_2$. Find $P_2$.
questions.solution_md: $P_1 = (-2, 6)$ (both signs change), then $P_2 = (-2, -6)$ (only the sign of the $y$-coordinate changes). Together the two steps act like a single reflection of $P$ in the $y$-axis. Option (a) stops at $P_1$.

questions.stem_md: The point $S(-3, 3)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $T$, in the origin to $U$, and in the $y$-axis to $V$. What kind of quadrilateral is $STUV$?

options.text_md: a rhombus with no right angle

questions.solution_md: $T(-3, -3)$, $U(3, -3)$, $V(3, 3)$. Each side is $6$ units long and is horizontal or vertical, so all four sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: $STUV$ is a square.

questions.stem_md: $K(5, 3)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $K'$. What is the area of triangle $OKK'$, where $O$ is the origin?
questions.solution_md: $K'$ is $(5, -3)$, so the base $KK' = 3 - (-3) = 6$ is vertical. The height is the distance of $O$ from the line $x = 5$, which is $5$. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 5 = 15$ square units. Option (c) forgets the half, (d) takes $3$ as the base, and (a) takes $3$ as the height.

questions.stem_md: How far apart are $S(-3, 4)$ and its mirror image in the $y$-axis?
questions.solution_md: The image is $(3, 4)$, on the same horizontal line, so the distance is $3 - (-3) = 6$ units: twice the distance of $S$ from the mirror. Option (d) doubles the $y$-coordinate, and (b) is the distance from $S$ to its image in the origin, $2 \times 5 = 10$.

questions.stem_md: Which rule gives the image of a point $(x, y)$ under reflection in the horizontal line $y = b$?
questions.solution_md: The $x$-coordinate does not change. The point is $y - b$ above the mirror, so its image is $y - b$ below it, at height $b - (y - b) = 2b - y$. Check with $b = 0$: the rule becomes $(x, -y)$, reflection in the $x$-axis. Option (a) changes the wrong coordinate.

questions.stem_md: How many points of the plane are left unchanged by reflection in the origin?
questions.solution_md: A fixed point needs $(x, y)$ and $(-x, -y)$ to be the same point, so $x = -x$ and $y = -y$, which forces $x = 0$ and $y = 0$: only the origin is invariant. A line mirror, by contrast, has infinitely many invariant points.

questions.stem_md: The segment $UV$ joins $U(1, 2)$ and $V(5, 5)$. It is reflected in the $x$-axis to $U'V'$. How long is $U'V'$?
questions.solution_md: $U'(1, -2)$ and $V'(5, -5)$, so $U'V' = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ units, the same as $UV$: a reflection does not change lengths. Options (c) and (d) are the vertical and horizontal gaps on their own, and (a) adds them: $4 + 3 = 7$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The image of $(-6, 4)$ in the $y$-axis is $(6, 4)$.

**Reason (R):** Reflection in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate and leaves the $y$-coordinate unchanged.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: $(-6, 4) \to (6, 4)$. R is the rule for reflection in the $y$-axis, and applying it gives A, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The point $(0, -5)$ is invariant under reflection in the $y$-axis.

**Reason (R):** Every point on the $x$-axis is its own image when the $y$-axis is the mirror.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: $(0, -5)$ lies on the $y$-axis, the mirror itself, so it does not move. R is false: a point such as $(3, 0)$ on the $x$-axis moves to $(-3, 0)$; only the origin stays fixed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reflecting $(3, 8)$ in the line $x = 5$ gives $(-3, 8)$.

**Reason (R):** A mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment that joins any point not on it to its image.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 5 - 3 = 7$, so the image is $(7, 8)$. The point $(-3, 8)$ is the image in the $y$-axis.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reflecting $(4, -9)$ in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis gives $(-4, 9)$.

**Reason (R):** A point and its image are always at the same distance from the mirror.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: $(4, -9) \to (4, 9) \to (-4, 9)$. R is also true, but A follows from the two coordinate rules (together they act as reflection in the origin), not from equal distances, so R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The point $(-2, 7)$ and its image in the line $y = 1$ are $12$ units apart.

**Reason (R):** If a point is $k$ units from a mirror line, then the point and its image are $2k$ units apart.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $(-2, 7)$ is $7 - 1 = 6$ units above the mirror, so by R the two points are $2 \times 6 = 12$ units apart; indeed the image is $(-2, -5)$. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reflection in the origin maps $(5, -1)$ to $(-5, 1)$.

**Reason (R):** Reflection in the origin has the same effect as one reflection in the $x$-axis.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: both signs change. R is false: reflection in the $x$-axis would give $(5, 1)$. Reflection in the origin equals reflection in the $x$-axis followed by reflection in the $y$-axis.

questions.stem_md: Reflecting a point twice in the same mirror line always brings it back to its starting position.
questions.solution_md: True. The second reflection undoes the first: in the line $x = 3$, $(8, 1) \to (-2, 1) \to (8, 1)$.

questions.stem_md: Reflection in the line $x = 3$ moves the point $(3, -4)$ to $(-3, -4)$.
questions.solution_md: False. $(3, -4)$ lies on the mirror $x = 3$, so it is invariant: the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 3 - 3 = 3$, and the image is $(3, -4)$ itself.

questions.stem_md: The point $(2, -5)$ ends up in the same place whether it is reflected in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis, or reflected once in the origin.
questions.solution_md: True. $(2, -5) \to (2, 5) \to (-2, 5)$, and reflection in the origin also gives $(-2, 5)$.

questions.stem_md: A triangle and its image under reflection in the $y$-axis can have different areas.
questions.solution_md: False. A reflection keeps every length, so the image is congruent to the triangle. For example, the triangle with vertices $(2, 1)$, $(6, 1)$, $(2, 4)$ and its image $(-2, 1)$, $(-6, 1)$, $(-2, 4)$ both have area $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6$ square units.

questions.stem_md: The point $(-1, 4)$ is its own image under reflection in the line $x = -1$.
questions.solution_md: True. It lies on the mirror line $x = -1$; the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times (-1) - (-1) = -1$.

questions.stem_md: Reflection in the line $y = -3$ sends $(0, 5)$ to $(0, -8)$.
questions.solution_md: False. $(0, 5)$ is $5 - (-3) = 8$ units above the mirror, so its image is $8$ units below it, at height $-3 - 8 = -11$: the image is $(0, -11)$. The value $-8$ comes from $-3 - 5 = -8$.

questions.stem_md: Under reflection in the $y$-axis, $(-8, -3)$ becomes $(k, -3)$, where $k$ = ___.
questions.solution_md: The rule $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$ changes only the sign of the $x$-coordinate, so $k = 8$.

questions.stem_md: When $(5, 2)$ is reflected in the vertical line $x = 1$, the $x$-coordinate of its image is ___.
questions.solution_md: The new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 1 - 5 = -3$, so the image is $(-3, 2)$.

questions.stem_md: The mirror line $y = 4$ maps $(-6, 1)$ to a point whose $y$-coordinate is ___.
questions.solution_md: The new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times 4 - 1 = 7$: the point is $3$ units below the mirror, so its image is $3$ units above it.

questions.stem_md: The only point that reflection in the origin leaves fixed is ___.
questions.solution_md: Only the origin $(0, 0)$ satisfies $(x, y) = (-x, -y)$.

questions.stem_md: If the image of $(4, -7)$ in the $x$-axis is written as $(4, k)$, the value of $k$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: Reflection in the $x$-axis changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate: $k = 7$.

questions.stem_md: $P(2, 9)$ and $P'(2, -3)$ are mirror images of each other in the line $y = c$. Then $c$ = ___.
questions.solution_md: The mirror lies halfway between them: $c = \dfrac{9 + (-3)}{2} = 3$.

questions.stem_md: Find the distance between $T(6, -8)$ and its image under reflection in the origin.
questions.solution_md: The image is $T'(-6, 8)$, and $O$ is the midpoint of $TT'$. $OT = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$, so $TT' = 2 \times 10 = 20$ units.

questions.stem_md: $P(4, 1)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $P'$ and in the $x$-axis to $P''$. Find the area of triangle $PP'P''$ in square units.
questions.solution_md: $P'(-4, 1)$ and $P''(4, -1)$. The angle at $P$ is a right angle ($PP'$ is horizontal and $PP''$ vertical), with $PP' = 4 - (-4) = 8$ and $PP'' = 1 - (-1) = 2$. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 2 = 8$ square units.

questions.stem_md: For what value of $k$ is the point $(k, -2)$ invariant under reflection in the line $x = 5$?
questions.solution_md: An invariant point is its own image: $2 \times 5 - k = k \Rightarrow 2k = 10 \Rightarrow k = 5$. (It lies on the mirror.)

questions.stem_md: The image of $(2a + 1, 6)$ in the $x$-axis is $(-5, 3b)$. Find the value of $a + b$.
questions.solution_md: Reflection in the $x$-axis gives $(2a + 1, -6)$. Comparing coordinates: $2a + 1 = -5 \Rightarrow a = -3$, and $3b = -6 \Rightarrow b = -2$. So $a + b = -3 + (-2) = -5$.

questions.stem_md: $A(4, 3)$ is reflected in the line $y = 1$ to $B$; $B$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $C$; and $D$ is the image of $A$ in the $y$-axis. Find the perimeter of the rectangle $ABCD$.
How far is the point $(-3, 7)$ from its image in the line $x = 2$?
questions.solution_md: The point is $2 - (-3) = 5$ units from the mirror, so it is $2 \times 5 = 10$ units from its image $(7, 7)$.

questions.stem_md: Under reflection in the line $y = -2$, the image of a point $G$ is $G'(5, -9)$. Find the length of $GG'$.
questions.solution_md: Reflect $G'$ back: the $y$-coordinate of $G$ is $2 \times (-2) - (-9) = 5$, so $G(5, 5)$. Then $GG' = 5 - (-9) = 14$ units.

questions.stem_md:
Write down the images of $A(-4, 6)$ under reflection in

(i) the $x$-axis,

(ii) the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The sign of the $y$-coordinate changes: the image is $(-4, -6)$.

(ii) Both signs change: the image is $(4, -6)$.

questions.solution_md: Use $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$ for the $x$-axis and $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$ for the origin.

questions.stem_md:
Find the image of $Q(9, -1)$ in

(i) the line $x = 6$,

(ii) the line $y = -4$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The $y$-coordinate stays $-1$; the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 6 - 9 = 3$. Image: $(3, -1)$.

(ii) The $x$-coordinate stays $9$; the new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times (-4) - (-1) = -7$. Image: $(9, -7)$.

questions.solution_md: In $x = a$ the image of $(x, y)$ is $(2a - x, y)$; in $y = b$ it is $(x, 2b - y)$.

questions.stem_md: A point $P$ is reflected in the $y$-axis, and its image is $(-2, -7)$. Find $P$, and then the image of $P$ in the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
Reflecting the image back in the $y$-axis gives $P(2, -7)$.

The image of $P$ in the origin is $(-2, 7)$.

questions.solution_md: A reflection undoes itself, so reflect the given image in the $y$-axis to recover $P$.

questions.stem_md:
Which of the points $A(0, 4)$, $B(4, 0)$ and $C(-4, 4)$ are invariant under reflection in

(i) the $y$-axis,

(ii) the line $y = 4$?

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Only $A$: it is the only one of the three with $x$-coordinate $0$, so it lies on the $y$-axis.

(ii) $A$ and $C$: both have $y$-coordinate $4$, so they lie on the mirror. $B$ moves to $(4, 8)$.

questions.solution_md: A point is invariant exactly when it lies on the mirror line.

questions.stem_md: $P(-5, -3)$ has image $P'(1, -3)$ in a mirror line. Find the mirror line, and the image of $(2, 8)$ in it.

answer.model_answer_md:
The $y$-coordinates are equal, so the mirror is vertical, halfway between: $\dfrac{-5 + 1}{2} = -2$. The mirror is the line $x = -2$.

Image of $(2, 8)$: the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times (-2) - 2 = -6$, so the image is $(-6, 8)$.

questions.solution_md: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$; then use $(x, y) \to (2a - x, y)$.

questions.stem_md:
$P(-4, 3)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $P'$, and $P'$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $P''$.

(i) Write the coordinates of $P'$ and $P''$.

(ii) Name the single transformation that maps $P$ to $P''$.

(iii) Find the length $PP''$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $P'(-4, -3)$ and $P''(4, -3)$.

(ii) Both coordinates of $P$ have changed sign, so the single transformation is reflection in the origin.

(iii) $O$ is the midpoint of $PP''$ and $OP = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$, so $PP'' = 2 \times 5 = 10$ units.

questions.solution_md: Apply the two axis rules one after the other; a change of both signs is reflection in the origin, which makes $O$ the midpoint.

questions.stem_md: $A(-1, 5)$ is reflected in the line $x = 2$ to $A'$, and $A'$ is reflected in the line $y = -1$ to $A''$. Find $A'$ and $A''$, and the area of triangle $AA'A''$.

answer.model_answer_md:
New $x$-coordinate in $x = 2$: $2 \times 2 - (-1) = 5$, so $A'(5, 5)$.

New $y$-coordinate in $y = -1$: $2 \times (-1) - 5 = -7$, so $A''(5, -7)$.

$AA'$ is horizontal and $A'A''$ vertical, so the angle at $A'$ is a right angle. $AA' = 5 - (-1) = 6$, $A'A'' = 5 - (-7) = 12$, and the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 = 36$ square units.

questions.solution_md: One mirror is vertical and the other horizontal, so the two segments $AA'$ and $A'A''$ are perpendicular legs of the triangle.

questions.stem_md: A point $P(a, b)$ is reflected in the origin to $P_1$, and $P_1$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $P_2(-6, 2)$. Find $a$ and $b$, and name the single reflection that maps $P$ to $P_2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Work backwards. Reflecting $P_2$ in the $x$-axis gives $P_1(-6, -2)$.

Reflecting $P_1$ in the origin gives $P(6, 2)$, so $a = 6$ and $b = 2$.

$P(6, 2)$ and $P_2(-6, 2)$ differ only in the sign of the $x$-coordinate, so the single reflection is in the $y$-axis.

questions.solution_md: Each reflection undoes itself, so undo the steps in reverse order; then compare $P$ with $P_2$.

questions.stem_md: The image of $(3p - 2, 4)$ under reflection in the line $y = 1$ is $(7, q + 3)$. Find $p$ and $q$.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $y = 1$ the $x$-coordinate is kept and the new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times 1 - 4 = -2$, so the image is $(3p - 2, -2)$.

Comparing $x$-coordinates: $3p - 2 = 7 \Rightarrow 3p = 9 \Rightarrow p = 3$.

Comparing $y$-coordinates: $q + 3 = -2 \Rightarrow q = -5$.

questions.solution_md: Write the image with the rule for $y = b$, then compare the coordinates one at a time.

questions.stem_md: Triangle $LMN$ has vertices $L(1, 2)$, $M(5, 2)$ and $N(1, 6)$. It is reflected in the line $x = -1$. Write the vertices of the image $L'M'N'$, and show that the two triangles have the same area.

answer.model_answer_md:
New $x$-coordinates: $2 \times (-1) - 1 = -3$ and $2 \times (-1) - 5 = -7$; the $y$-coordinates are kept. So $L'(-3, 2)$, $M'(-7, 2)$, $N'(-3, 6)$.

In each triangle one side is horizontal and one vertical, of lengths $4$ and $4$.

So each area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 4 = 8$ square units: the areas are equal, as a reflection keeps lengths.

questions.solution_md: Reflect each vertex with $(x, y) \to (2a - x, y)$; the image triangle is congruent to the original.

questions.stem_md:
On graph paper, plot $A(4, 2)$. Reflect $A$ in the $x$-axis to get $B$, and reflect $B$ in the origin to get $C$.

(i) Write the coordinates of $B$ and $C$.

(ii) Name triangle $ABC$ and find its area.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $B(4, -2)$ and $C(-4, 2)$.

(ii) $AB$ is vertical and $AC$ is horizontal, so the angle at $A$ is a right angle: $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle.

$AB = 2 - (-2) = 4$ and $AC = 4 - (-4) = 8$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 8 = 16$ square units.

questions.solution_md: Plot each point as it is found; the right angle shows at once because one leg is vertical and the other horizontal.

questions.stem_md:
Triangle $PQR$ has vertices $P(1, 1)$, $Q(4, 1)$ and $R(1, 3)$. It is reflected in the line $y = 1$.

(i) Which vertices are invariant?

(ii) Write the image $R'$ of $R$.

(iii) Name the figure $RQR'$ and find its area.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $P$ and $Q$ have $y$-coordinate $1$, so they lie on the mirror and are invariant.

(ii) The new $y$-coordinate of $R$ is $2 \times 1 - 3 = -1$, so $R'(1, -1)$.

(iii) $QR = QR'$ (a reflection keeps lengths), so $RQR'$ is an isosceles triangle. Its base $RR' = 3 - (-1) = 4$ lies on the line $x = 1$, and its height is the distance of $Q$ from that line, $4 - 1 = 3$.

Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6$ square units.

questions.solution_md: Vertices on the mirror stay where they are; the triangle and its image together make a figure that is symmetric about the mirror.

questions.stem_md:
The point $P(5, -2)$ is reflected in a line $l$ to $P'(-1, -2)$.

(i) Find the equation of $l$.

(ii) Find the image of $Q(-4, 7)$ in $l$.

(iii) Give two points of $l$ that are invariant under this reflection.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $P$ and $P'$ have the same $y$-coordinate, so $l$ is vertical and passes through the midpoint of $PP'$: $\dfrac{5 + (-1)}{2} = 2$. So $l$ is $x = 2$.

(ii) New $x$-coordinate: $2 \times 2 - (-4) = 8$; the $y$-coordinate stays $7$. The image of $Q$ is $(8, 7)$.

(iii) Every point of $l$ is invariant, for example $(2, 0)$ and $(2, -2)$ (the midpoint of $PP'$).

questions.solution_md: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$; then reflect $Q$ in it; invariant points are exactly the points on the mirror.

questions.stem_md:
$A(-2, 3)$ is reflected in the line $x = 1$ to $B$, and $B$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $C$.

(i) Find $B$ and $C$.

(ii) Find the single mirror line that reflects $A$ directly onto $C$.

(iii) Find the lengths $AB$ and $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) New $x$-coordinate in $x = 1$: $2 \times 1 - (-2) = 4$, so $B(4, 3)$; then in the $y$-axis $C(-4, 3)$.

(ii) $A$ and $C$ have the same $y$-coordinate, so the mirror is vertical, through the midpoint: $\dfrac{-2 + (-4)}{2} = -3$. The line is $x = -3$.

(iii) All three points lie on the line $y = 3$: $AB = 4 - (-2) = 6$ units and $BC = 4 - (-4) = 8$ units.

questions.solution_md: Two reflections in parallel lines move a point along the same horizontal line; a single mirror for $A$ and $C$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AC$.

questions.stem_md:
The point $(m, 2m - 1)$ has image $(-4, n)$ under reflection in the $y$-axis.

(i) Find $m$ and $n$.

(ii) Find the distance between the point and its image.

(iii) Write the image of the point under reflection in the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The $y$-axis image of $(m, 2m - 1)$ is $(-m, 2m - 1)$. Comparing: $-m = -4 \Rightarrow m = 4$, and $n = 2m - 1 = 2 \times 4 - 1 = 7$. The point is $(4, 7)$.

(ii) The point $(4, 7)$ and its image $(-4, 7)$ lie on the same horizontal line, so the distance is $4 - (-4) = 8$ units.

(iii) Reflection in the origin gives $(-4, -7)$.

questions.solution_md: Write the image with the $y$-axis rule and compare coordinates; then use the coordinates found.

questions.stem_md:
The segment joining $E(2, 5)$ and $F(5, 1)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $E'F'$.

(i) Write the coordinates of $E'$ and $F'$.

(ii) Name the figure $EFF'E'$.

(iii) Find its area and its perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $E'(-2, 5)$ and $F'(-5, 1)$.

(ii) $EE'$ and $FF'$ are both horizontal, so they are parallel, while $EF = E'F'$ (a reflection keeps lengths): $EFF'E'$ is an isosceles trapezium.

(iii) $EE' = 2 - (-2) = 4$, $FF' = 5 - (-5) = 10$, and the distance between these parallel sides is $5 - 1 = 4$. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (4 + 10) \times 4 = 28$ square units.

$EF = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so the perimeter is $4 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 24$ units.

questions.solution_md: The two parallel sides are the horizontal segments $EE'$ and $FF'$; the slanted sides are a segment and its image, so they are equal.

questions.stem_md:
Use graph paper for this question (take $1$ cm $= 1$ unit on both axes).

(a) Plot $P(4, 3)$ and $Q(1, -2)$. Reflect both points in the $y$-axis to get $P'$ and $Q'$, and write their coordinates.

(b) Name the figure $PQQ'P'$ and find its area.

(c) $P'$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $P''$. Name the single transformation that maps $P$ to $P''$, and find the length $PP''$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $P'(-4, 3)$ and $Q'(-1, -2)$ (the sign of the $x$-coordinate changes).

**(b)** $PP'$ and $QQ'$ are both horizontal, so they are parallel; $PQ = P'Q'$ because a reflection keeps lengths. So $PQQ'P'$ is an isosceles trapezium. $PP' = 4 - (-4) = 8$, $QQ' = 1 - (-1) = 2$, and the distance between them is $3 - (-2) = 5$. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (8 + 2) \times 5 = 25$ square units.

**(c)** $P''(-4, -3)$. Both coordinates of $P$ have changed sign, so the single transformation is reflection in the origin. $O$ is the midpoint of $PP''$ and $OP = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$, so $PP'' = 2 \times 5 = 10$ units.

questions.solution_md: Reflect each point with the y-axis rule; the parallel sides of the trapezium are the horizontal segments PP′ and QQ′; two reflections in the axes make one reflection in the origin.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) The point $A(-3, 2)$ is reflected in the line $x = 1$ to $B$, and $B$ is reflected in the line $y = -1$ to $C$. Write the coordinates of $B$ and $C$.

(b) Name triangle $ABC$ and find its area.

(c) $D$ is the image of $A$ in the line $y = -1$. Name the quadrilateral $ABCD$, find its perimeter, and find the length of the diagonal $AC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In $x = 1$ the new $x$-coordinate is $2 \times 1 - (-3) = 5$, so $B(5, 2)$. In $y = -1$ the new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times (-1) - 2 = -4$, so $C(5, -4)$.

**(b)** $AB$ is horizontal and $BC$ is vertical, so the angle at $B$ is a right angle: $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle. $AB = 5 - (-3) = 8$, $BC = 2 - (-4) = 6$, and the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24$ square units.

**(c)** $D(-3, -4)$. All four angles of $ABCD$ are right angles and $AB \ne BC$, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle. Perimeter $= 2 \times (8 + 6) = 28$ units. $AC = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ units.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) The point $P(a, b)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $P'(5, -3)$. Find $a$ and $b$.

(b) Write the image $P''$ of $P$ in the line $x = 2$. Find the point where the segment $PP''$ meets the line $x = 2$, and say why that point is invariant under this reflection.

(c) Name triangle $PP'P''$, giving a reason, and find its area.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Reflecting $P'$ back in the $x$-axis gives $P(5, 3)$, so $a = 5$ and $b = 3$.

**(b)** New $x$-coordinate: $2 \times 2 - 5 = -1$, so $P''(-1, 3)$. The line $x = 2$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PP''$, so they meet at the midpoint $(2, 3)$. It lies on the mirror, and points on the mirror are invariant.

**(c)** $PP'$ is vertical and $PP''$ horizontal, so the angle at $P$ is a right angle. $PP' = 3 - (-3) = 6$ and $PP'' = 5 - (-1) = 6$ are equal, so $PP'P''$ is a right-angled isosceles triangle. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 6 = 18$ square units.

questions.solution_md: Undo the x-axis reflection to find P; the mirror x = 2 bisects PP″ at right angles; the two legs from P are perpendicular and equal.

marking_scheme.step: (b) invariant because it is on the mirror

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) $A(-3, 4)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $A_1$, and $A_1$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to $A_2$. Write the coordinates of $A_1$ and $A_2$.

(b) $A_3$ is the image of $A$ under reflection in the origin. Write $A_3$, compare it with $A_2$, and state the single transformation equivalent to the two reflections in (a).

(c) Name triangle $AA_1A_2$, and find its area and the length $AA_2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $A_1(3, 4)$ and $A_2(3, -4)$.

**(b)** $A_3(3, -4)$, the same point as $A_2$. So reflection in the $y$-axis followed by reflection in the $x$-axis is equivalent to a single reflection in the origin.

**(c)** $AA_1$ is horizontal and $A_1A_2$ is vertical, so $AA_1A_2$ is a right-angled triangle with the right angle at $A_1$. $AA_1 = 3 - (-3) = 6$ and $A_1A_2 = 4 - (-4) = 8$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24$ square units, and $AA_2 = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ units.

questions.solution_md: Apply the axis rules in turn; both signs change, which is the rule for the origin; the legs of the triangle are the horizontal and vertical moves.

questions.stem_md:
Use graph paper for this question (take $1$ cm $= 1$ unit on both axes).

(a) Plot $A(6, 0)$, $B(3, 4)$ and $C(-3, 0)$. Reflect $B$ in the $x$-axis to get $D$, and write its coordinates. Which of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are invariant under this reflection?

(b) Name the quadrilateral $ABCD$, giving a reason.

(c) Find the length $AB$ and the area of $ABCD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $D(3, -4)$. $A$ and $C$ lie on the $x$-axis, the mirror, so they are invariant; $B$ is not.

**(b)** The mirror maps $B$ to $D$ and fixes $A$ and $C$, so $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$: two pairs of equal adjacent sides. As $AB \ne CB$, $ABCD$ is a kite (with $AC$ as its axis of symmetry).

**(c)** $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ units. The diagonals are $AC = 6 - (-3) = 9$ and $BD = 4 - (-4) = 8$, and they are perpendicular, so the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 8 = 36$ square units. (Check: triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ each have base $9$ and height $4$: $2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 4 = 36$.)

questions.solution_md: Points on the mirror are invariant; a figure made of a point, its image and two invariant points is symmetric about the mirror; a kite has perpendicular diagonals, so its area is half their product.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) The image of $P(-2, 7)$ in a line $l$ is $P'(-2, -1)$. Find the equation of $l$.

(b) Find the images of $Q(5, -2)$ and $R(-4, 3)$ in $l$. What do you notice about $R$?

(c) The point $(2k - 1, k + 2)$ is invariant under reflection in $l$. Find $k$, the point, and the image of the point in the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $P$ and $P'$ have the same $x$-coordinate, so $l$ is horizontal, halfway between them: $\dfrac{7 + (-1)}{2} = 3$. So $l$ is $y = 3$.

**(b)** For $Q$ the new $y$-coordinate is $2 \times 3 - (-2) = 8$, so its image is $(5, 8)$. $R$ has $y$-coordinate $3$, so it lies on $l$: its image is $(-4, 3)$ itself, an invariant point.

**(c)** An invariant point lies on $l$, so its $y$-coordinate is $3$: $k + 2 = 3 \Rightarrow k = 1$. Its $x$-coordinate is then $2 \times 1 - 1 = 1$, so the point is $(1, 3)$, and its image in the origin is $(-1, -3)$.

questions.solution_md: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of PP′; a point is invariant exactly when it lies on the mirror.

questions.stem_md:
Use graph paper for this question (take $1$ cm $= 1$ unit on both axes).

(a) Draw triangle $ABC$ with $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(4, 5)$. Reflect it in the $y$-axis and write the vertices of its image $A'B'C'$.

(b) Name the quadrilateral $BCC'B'$ and find its area.

(c) Find the perimeter and the area of triangle $ABC$. Without measuring, state the perimeter and area of $A'B'C'$, giving a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $A'(-1, 1)$, $B'(-4, 1)$, $C'(-4, 5)$.

**(b)** $BC$ and $B'C'$ are vertical, $CC'$ and $BB'$ horizontal, so every angle is a right angle; $BB' = 4 - (-4) = 8$ and $BC = 5 - 1 = 4$ are unequal, so $BCC'B'$ is a rectangle. Area $= 8 \times 4 = 32$ square units.

**(c)** $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$ and $AC = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so the perimeter is $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ units, and the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6$ square units (right angle at $B$). Triangle $A'B'C'$ also has perimeter $12$ units and area $6$ square units, because a reflection does not change lengths: the image is congruent to $ABC$.

questions.solution_md: Reflect each vertex in the y-axis; vertical and horizontal sides give right angles; a reflection keeps every length, so the image triangle is congruent.
